desc:
You are given a binary search tree with distinct values and an integer target. Run the standard BST search: start at the root; at every node, stop if its value equals target, go to the left child if target is smaller, and go to the right child if it is larger. The search also stops when it tries to move to a missing child.

Return the number of nodes the search looked at (the node that matches counts, a missing child does not). The empty tree gives 0.

Tree encoding. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level order. The first entry is the root. After that, the left and right child of every existing node are written in turn, level by level, from left to right. A missing child is written as -1 (node values are never negative, so -1 cannot be confused with a value). Missing nodes have no children listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped. The empty tree is [].

For example, [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14] is the tree whose root 8 has children 3 and 10; node 3 has children 1 and 6; node 10 has no left child and right child 14.

Example 1

tree = [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14,-1,-1,4,7,13], target = 4
Output: 4
The search looks at 8, 3, 6 and 4.

Example 2

tree = [8,3,10,1,6,-1,14,-1,-1,4,7,13], target = 20
Output: 3
The search looks at 8, 10 and 14, then 14 has no right child.

Example 3

tree = [], target = 5
Output: 0
constraints: 0 ≤ node value ≤ 100,000, all values distinct; the tree is a valid BST
0 ≤ target ≤ 100,000 (target may or may not be in the tree)
hints: Each comparison discards one whole side of the tree, so you never need to look at more than one root-to-leaf path.
Keep a pointer to the current node and a counter. Increase the counter every time you step onto a real node.
Loop while the current node exists: count it, stop if it equals the target, otherwise move to the left or right child. Remember the empty tree.
editorial: A BST search follows a single path from the root. Decode the level-order array into explicit left and right child indices, then walk: count the current node, return the count if the value matches, otherwise move left when target < value and right when it is larger. If the child you need is missing the walk ends and the count so far is the answer.
The walk visits at most one node per level, so it costs O(h) after the O(n) decoding step (h is the height of the tree). The extra memory is the decoded child arrays, O(n).
